newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bomb explodes by Algerian school, no casualties.
newsitem.headline: Bomb explodes by Algerian school, no casualties.

text.p: A bomb exploded on Monday outside a school for girls in a suburb southeast of the capital Algiers, but there were no casualties and only slight material damage, residents said.
The explosion by Ourida Meddad high school in El Harrach area came about 14 hours after a powerful car bomb ripped through an Algiers avenue killing 23 people and wounding 100.

The latest blast follows a pattern of attacks against schools since 1994 when the ruthless Armed Islamic Group (GIA) warned students to stay away from schools, arguing their courses hamper the struggle to overthrow the government.
More than 800 schools were burnt down in a campaign of sabotage since, with more than 450 students and teachers killed.
A leading Algerian newspaper on Monday called Sunday's car bombing in Algiers a "Ramadan massacre".
State-run television showed footage of mangled cars, wrecked buildings and debris strewn over more than 200 metres in the working-class Belouizdad avenue.
"Only 10 people among the dead have been identified so far...The other bodies were so badly mutilated," said a hospital nurse by telephone from Algiers.
A doctor in Algiers's Mustapha hospital, speaking by telephone, said of Sunday's bomb: "It was one of the worst bombings in Algiers since 1995 because of the casualties."
Algiers experienced its deadliest bombing in 1995 when Moslem guerrillas slammed a car laden with explosives into a police station killing more than 40 and wounding more than 300.

At least 100 people have been killed and more than 150 wounded in the first 10 days of the Moslem holy month of Ramadan in Algeria as fundamentalist guerrillas seek to disprove government claims that it has crushed their revolt.
Sunday's bomb followed a massacre of dozens of villagers in Medea province, a stronghold of the feared GIA.

The leading Algerian newspaper Liberte said guerrillas raided the village of Sidi Abdelaziz 70 km (40 miles) south of Algiers, in the early hours of Sunday and slit the throats of 48 villagers, including women and children. The government put the death toll at 36.
Liberte dubbed the killings "Ramadan massacres", referring to the month in which Moslem guerrillas usually step up attacks against the Algerian government.

Analysts believed the killings were a message to President Liamine Zeroual as well as to mainstream Algerians that the fundamentalists are still a formidable force despite repeated claims by the government that it has crushed the guerrillas.
Zeroual reasserted this week his government was committed to wiping out the guerrillas.

"One theory is that it is a statement -- sort of Ramadan message -- to the authorities and to the public that the rebels are still very much able to operate," said an analyst in Algiers who did not want to be identified.
The attacks appear indiscriminate, hitting even areas which are associated with the guerrillas.
"These massacres have no message but killing for the sake of killing..." said Liberte newspaper.
About 60,000 people have been killed in civil violence in Algeria since the cancellation in 1992 of a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
